transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I’m here because there’s been this situation with my ensemble. For almost two years now, I haven’t been able to shake the feeling—well, the certainty—that after a commission, a few people started quietly working against me.

It’s small things. Schedule changes, where people are seated, little comments in rehearsal. They’ll show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it, but it doesn’t really change what I’m seeing.

During this two-year period, have you had any distinct episodes where your mood was unusually high, energetic, or irritable, or conversely very low and depressed, that lasted for days to weeks at a time?

I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had good days and bad days, like anyone, and I’ve been frustrated at times. But I wouldn’t say there were stretches where my mood was… extreme for days or weeks. Not that I’ve noticed.
Aside from these suspicions, have you ever heard voices or sounds that others couldn't hear, or seen things that others didn't see?
No… I don’t think so. I haven’t really had anything like that, not that I’ve noticed.

Aside from this situation with your ensemble, would you say you've generally had a hard time trusting people—friends, family, or others—throughout most of your adult life, even before this all started?
Not really… I mean, I’ve always been a little careful with people, I guess. But I wouldn’t say I had some lifelong problem trusting everyone before this.
Aside from this situation with your colleagues, how have things been going for you overall—are you still able to keep up with your daily routines, work, and relationships as usual?

Mostly, yeah. I still get my work done… deadlines and composing and all that. I run most mornings. Things with my wife are basically steady. It’s really just the ensemble situation that’s been… difficult.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that ensemble colleagues are conspiring against him) persisting for approximately two years. There is no evidence of hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior, or other psychotic symptoms characteristic of schizophrenia. Mood episodes (mania/depression) were explicitly denied, ruling out a mood disorder with psychotic features. There is no lifelong pattern of pervasive distrust predating the current belief system, arguing against paranoid personality disorder. Notably, overall functioning—work, marriage, daily routines—remains largely intact except for the circumscribed area of the delusion, which is classic for Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia, where functional decline and broader symptomatology are expected.
